title: Room Climate Display
pitch: A desk screen that shows the room's temperature and humidity, with a little comfort message.

guide.about: Read a DHT11 sensor and print the values on a 16x2 LCD that only needs 4 wires thanks to its I2C backpack. You'll install and use your first libraries.
parts: with the I2C backpack soldered on
wiring: the Uno also has SDA/SCL pins near AREF: same signals
steps: Install the libraries listed in the Code section (Tools → Manage Libraries).
Wire the DHT11 module: + to 5V, − to GND, DATA to Pin 2.
Wire the LCD backpack: GND, VCC to 5V, SDA to A4, SCL to A5.
Upload the code.
If the screen lights but shows nothing, slowly turn the blue screw on the back (contrast) with a small screwdriver.
Still blank? Change LCD_ADDRESS in the code from 0x27 to 0x3F and upload again.
guide.test: Line 1 shows temperature and humidity, line 2 shows a message like "Comfy :)" or "Too humid!". Breathe on the sensor and the humidity jumps up.
next: Swap in a DHT22 for more accuracy (change DHTTYPE to DHT22).
Add a buzzer that warns when the room gets too hot.

title: Mini Weather Station
pitch: Big crisp numbers on an OLED screen plus a kaomoji face that reacts to the weather. (^_^)

guide.about: Combine an accurate DHT22 sensor with a 128x64 OLED. You'll learn how to draw text in different sizes and update the screen without flicker.
wiring: check the pin labels: VCC and GND order differs between sellers!
steps: Install the four libraries from the Code section.
Read the labels printed on your OLED's pins before wiring. Some are GND-VCC-SCL-SDA, others VCC-GND-SCL-SDA.
Wire the OLED: VCC to 5V, GND to GND, SCL to A5, SDA to A4.
Wire the DHT22: + to 5V, − to GND, DATA to Pin 2.
Upload the code. The screen shows "Warming up…" for 2 seconds, then the readings.
guide.test: You see the temperature in big digits, humidity below it, and a face: (^_^) comfy, (>_<) hot, (o_o) cold, (~_~) humid.
next: Log min/max temperature of the day.
Add a BMP280 for air pressure (needs a 3.3V supply or a 3.3V board).

title: Garage Parking Assistant
pitch: Beeps faster and faster as you get closer, and lights red when it's time to stop. Like a real car sensor.

guide.about: The ultrasonic sensor sends a sound pulse and times the echo. The code turns that time into centimetres, then maps the distance to beep speed and LED color.
parts: or RCWL-1601: same pins, both fine at 5V
220Ω for each LED and one for the buzzer
wiring: 5V boards only: on an ESP32 this would need a divider
steps: Place the ultrasonic sensor at the edge of the breadboard with its "eyes" facing out.
Wire VCC to 5V, GND to GND, TRIG to Pin 7 and ECHO to Pin 6.
Wire the buzzer through a 220Ω resistor to Pin 8 and − to GND.
(Optional) Add the three LEDs, each with a 220Ω resistor, to pins 2, 3 and 4.
Upload the code and open the Serial Monitor at 9600 to see the distance.
Move your hand toward the sensor and listen.
guide.test: Over 100 cm: quiet and green. 100–30 cm: beeps speed up, yellow. Under 30 cm: red and a solid tone. Change STOP_CM in the code to match your garage.
next: Mount it on the garage wall at bumper height, powered by a USB charger.
Show the distance on a TM1637 display.

title: Ultrasonic Tape Measure
pitch: Point it at a wall to measure distance on a 16x2 LCD, with no tape needed. Great for room planning.

guide.about: Wire a plain (non-I2C) 16x2 LCD in 4-bit mode: more wires, but you'll understand exactly how the screen is driven. A button freezes the reading.
wiring: pot outer legs go to 5V and GND
we only write to the screen
steps: Push the LCD's 16 pins into the breadboard (solder header pins on first if it came without).
Wire power: pin 1 to GND, pin 2 to 5V, pin 16 to GND and pin 15 to 5V through a 220Ω resistor.
Add the potentiometer: outer legs to 5V and GND, middle leg to LCD pin 3.
Wire RS, RW, E and D4–D7 exactly as in the table (D0–D3, pins 7–10, stay empty).
Upload the code, then turn the potentiometer until the text is sharp.
Wire the ultrasonic sensor (TRIG 9, ECHO 10) and the optional HOLD button on Pin 7.
Point the sensor at a wall and read the distance.
guide.test: The LCD shows the distance in cm and inches, updating 4 times a second. Holding the button freezes the value and shows HOLD.
safety: Soldering header pins: the iron tip is about 350°C. Use the stand and solder in a ventilated room.
next: Add a "zero" button that measures from the back of the device.
Average 5 readings for steadier numbers.

title: Intruder Alarm
pitch: A motion-sensing room alarm with a siren sound. Arm and disarm it with a button.

guide.about: The PIR sensor notices body heat moving. When the alarm is armed and something moves, a rising-and-falling siren plays. A button arms and disarms it, with a 10-second exit delay.
parts: 220Ω for the buzzer and the LED
steps: Look at the PIR: set the jumper to "H" (repeat trigger) if it has one. Turn both orange knobs to the middle.
Wire the PIR: VCC to 5V, OUT to Pin 2, GND to GND.
Wire the buzzer through 220Ω to Pin 8.
(Optional) Button on Pin 4 to GND, red LED with 220Ω on Pin 13.
Upload, then wait about 1 minute: the PIR needs to settle after power-up.
Press the button to arm (the LED blinks for 10 s, then stays on). Walk past it!
guide.test: Armed + motion = siren for 10 seconds. Press the button to disarm. Without a button, the alarm arms itself 10 s after power-up.
next: Add a keypad to disarm with a secret code.
Use an ESP32 instead and send a notification to your phone.

title: Thirsty Plant Alert
pitch: Your plant tells you when it's thirsty: green means happy, red plus a little chirp means "water me!"

guide.about: A capacitive sensor measures soil moisture without rusting. You'll calibrate it (record a dry and a wet reading) so the plant's mood is accurate.
parts: 220Ω for each LED and the buzzer
power from a USB charger near the plant
steps: Wire the soil sensor: VCC 5V, GND, AOUT to A0.
Add the LEDs with 220Ω resistors on pins 5 (green) and 6 (red).
Upload the code and open the Serial Monitor at 9600.
Calibrate: hold the sensor in the air and note the number (dry). Put it in a glass of water up to the line, not deeper, and note the number (wet).
Type those numbers into DRY_VALUE and WET_VALUE in the code and upload again.
Push the sensor into the soil up to the white line, keeping the top electronics dry.
guide.test: The Serial Monitor shows moisture in %. Above 40%: green. Below 30%: red, plus a short chirp every 10 minutes if you added the buzzer.
safety: Keep the board and USB away from water; only the sensor's blade goes into the soil.
next: Add a pump to water it automatically (see the Auto Plant Waterer idea).
Use a WS2812B ring as a mood light around the pot.

title: Clap Clap Lamp
pitch: Clap twice to turn the light on, clap twice again to turn it off. Pure magic for guests.

guide.about: The sound module's DO pin flips when a sound is louder than the level set by its screw. The code looks for two loud sounds 150–700 ms apart: a double clap.
steps: Wire the sound module: + to 5V, G to GND, D0 to Pin 2.
Add the LED with its 220Ω resistor on Pin 9.
Upload and open the Serial Monitor at 9600.
Tune: in a quiet room turn the module's screw until its second LED is just OFF. A clap should flash it.
Clap twice quickly!
guide.test: A double clap toggles the LED and prints "Double clap!". Single claps and talking are ignored. If nothing reacts, turn the screw a little more sensitive.
next: Switch a relay to control a 12V lamp.
Triple clap for a party blink mode.

title: Smoke Sniffer (demo)
pitch: An MQ-2 gas sensor that beeps when it smells smoke or lighter gas. A fun science demo.

guide.about: The MQ-2 has a tiny heater, and its resistance drops when it smells smoke or flammable gas. The code measures "normal air" at startup and alarms when the reading rises well above it.
wiring: the heater needs 5V and ~150mA: fine from USB
5V boards only: the output can reach 5V
steps: Wire the MQ-2: VCC 5V, GND, A0 to A0.
Wire the buzzer through 220Ω to Pin 8.
Upload the code. The sensor warms up for 60 seconds (it gets warm, that's normal), then measures clean air.
Open the Serial Monitor at 9600 to watch the values.
Test: hold an unlit lighter near it and press the gas button for 1 second (don't light it). The alarm should sound.
guide.test: Clean air shows a steady number. A puff of lighter gas pushes it up and triggers beeping plus the LED.
safety: This is NOT a safety device. Never rely on it instead of a real smoke or gas alarm.
Never use open flames near the sensor indoors; test only with unlit lighter gas, briefly, in a ventilated room.
The sensor's metal mesh gets hot. Don't touch it while it's running.
next: Show the reading as a bar graph on an LCD.
Log readings to an SD card to see air changes over a day.

title: Tilt Ball Collector
pitch: Tilt the breadboard to roll a ball across a tiny OLED screen and collect stars. A real motion-controlled game!

guide.about: Read the MPU-6050's accelerometer directly over I2C (saving memory), turn tilt into ball speed, and draw a mini game on the OLED. Both modules share the same two I2C wires.
wiring: the GY-521 has its own 3.3V regulator
steps: Install Adafruit SSD1306 and Adafruit GFX Library.
Place the MPU-6050 flat on the breadboard (it should move with the board).
Wire both modules to 5V and GND, and connect both SDA pins to A4 and both SCL pins to A5.
Upload the code and keep the breadboard flat for the first second (it calibrates).
Tilt the breadboard to roll the ball onto the stars!
guide.test: The ball rolls toward the low side and bounces off walls. Touching a star adds a point and a new star appears. Collect 10 for a victory screen.
next: Add holes that reset the score.
Add a passive buzzer for collect sounds.

title: Speedrun Stopwatch
pitch: A big 4-digit stopwatch for timing game runs, Rubik's cubes or homework sprints. One button starts and stops it, another resets.

guide.about: Use millis() to time things precisely and show seconds plus hundredths, then minutes and seconds, on a TM1637 display with a blinking colon.
parts: or arcade buttons: START/STOP and RESET
steps: Install the TM1637 library by Avishay Orpaz.
Wire the display: VCC 5V, GND, CLK to Pin 3, DIO to Pin 4.
Wire the two buttons to pins 2 and 5 (other legs to GND).
Upload the code.
Press START, then press again to stop. RESET clears it (only while stopped).
guide.test: Under a minute it shows SS:hh (seconds and hundredths), after a minute MM:SS. The colon blinks while running.
next: Add a split-time button.
Use an arcade button for a satisfying slam-to-stop.

title: Always-Right Desk Clock
pitch: A 4-digit clock that keeps perfect time even when unplugged, thanks to its coin-cell clock chip.

guide.about: The DS3231 real-time clock counts time on its own battery. On the first upload, the code copies your PC's time into it. After that it never forgets.
parts: check the coin-cell note in its part info
steps: Install RTClib (by Adafruit) and TM1637 (by Avishay Orpaz).
Put a coin cell in the DS3231 (see its part info about rechargeable vs normal cells).
Wire the DS3231 to 5V, GND, SDA A4, SCL A5.
Wire the TM1637 to 5V, GND, CLK 3, DIO 4.
Upload the code. If the clock had no time yet, it takes the time from your PC.
To force a new time later, set FORCE_SET_TIME to true, upload, then set it back to false and upload again.
guide.test: The display shows HH:MM with a blinking colon. Unplug USB for a minute and plug back in: the time is still right.
safety: Coin cells are dangerous if swallowed. Keep them away from small children.
next: Add a buzzer alarm at a set time.
Show the temperature (the DS3231 has a built-in thermometer!) every 10 seconds.

title: Secret Code Safe
pitch: Type the right 4-digit code on a keypad and a servo unlocks the latch. Wrong code? Red light and a buzz.

guide.about: Read a 4x4 keypad matrix, build up the typed code in memory, and drive a servo as a lock bolt. Press * to clear and # to submit.
parts: 220Ω for each LED and the buzzer
wiring: left to right, looking at the keys
one SG90 is OK on the board's 5V pin
steps: Install the Keypad library (by Mark Stanley) and Servo.
Plug the keypad's 8-wire ribbon into male jumpers. Pins 1–4 go to 9, 8, 7, 6 and pins 5–8 go to 5, 4, 3, 2.
Wire the servo: brown GND, red 5V, orange to Pin 10.
(Optional) Add the LEDs and buzzer with 220Ω resistors.
Change SECRET in the code to your own 4-digit code, then upload.
Type the code and press #.
guide.test: Correct code: green light, happy beep, servo turns to 90° (unlocked) for 5 seconds, then locks again. Wrong code: red light and a low buzz. Open the Serial Monitor (9600) to see keys as you press them.
safety: One SG90 can run from the board's 5V pin. If the board resets when the servo moves, give the servo a separate 5V supply (connect the grounds).
next: Build it into a cardboard box with the servo arm as the latch.
Lock everyone out for 30 s after 3 wrong tries.

title: Knob-to-Servo Gauge
pitch: Turn a knob and a servo pointer follows it. The start of every robot arm and dashboard gauge.

guide.about: A servo moves to whatever angle you write. Map a knob's 0–1023 range to 0–180°, smooth it, and you have precise control.
steps: Install the Servo library if it isn't there yet.
Wire the servo: brown GND, red 5V, orange Pin 9.
Wire the potentiometer: outer legs to 5V and GND, middle to A0.
Upload and turn the knob.
Tape a paper arrow to the servo horn and draw a scale behind it.
guide.test: The servo follows the knob smoothly from 0° to 180°.
safety: If the board resets or the servo jitters, power the servo from a separate 5V supply (connect grounds).
next: Replace the knob with a light sensor: a gauge that points at the brightness.
Add a second servo + joystick for a pan-tilt mount.

title: Photo Turntable
pitch: A slow, precise turntable that rotates your figure or model in 12 steps so you can snap perfect 360° photos.

guide.about: The 28BYJ-48 stepper moves in tiny, exact steps (about 2048 per turn). The code turns 30° at a time, waits 3 seconds for your photo, and repeats 12 times. Perfect for anime figure photography!
parts: driver board, usually sold with the motor
wiring: fine for testing; use a separate 5V supply for long sessions
steps: Install the Stepper library.
Plug the motor's white connector into the ULN2003 board.
Wire IN1–IN4 to pins 8, 9, 10, 11 (the code handles the special order this motor needs).
Power the driver: + to 5V and − to GND.
Upload. Press the button (or wait 5 s if you have none) to start a 12-shot rotation.
Glue a jar lid or cardboard disc to the motor shaft as the turntable plate.
guide.test: The ULN2003's 4 LEDs flicker as it moves 30°, pauses 3 s (snap a photo!), and repeats until a full circle is done.
safety: Never wire the stepper directly to board pins: always through the ULN2003 driver.
If the board resets during moves, power the driver from a separate 5V supply and connect its GND to the board GND.
next: Add a passive buzzer that beeps when it's time to shoot.
Use an IR remote to trigger each step.
